message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review was carried out rigorously and, importantly, independently: the contractor's delay analysis was tested and agreed by our independent project manager, so the allocation of the 70 days of delay is not just the contractor's version. The findings are clear. The single biggest cause was the unforeseen ground conditions, which trace back to a thin site investigation, and the recommendation on full-footprint investigations addresses that head on. The commercial position is equally clear: the contractor carries 14 days, so we recover £45,000 in liquidated damages, and the overrun is explained by identifiable causes. The review also looks beyond this one project. By comparing all our education projects since 2022, we found that two-stage tendering is associated with delays a third as long as single-stage, which gives us an evidence-based case for changing our default procurement route. Every recommendation is specific and actionable. I believe the review gives Members a fair, well-documented account and a sound basis for improving future projects.
</author>

<document>
Project Review: Delay to Practical Completion, Riverside Primary School Extension
Capital Projects Team, Mereford Council, November 2026

1. Purpose
This review explains why the Riverside Primary School extension reached practical completion ten weeks late, sets out the commercial position with the contractor, and draws lessons for the Council's capital programme.

2. Project summary
The project added a four-classroom teaching block and a new hall to Riverside Primary School. The contract was let on a single-stage design and build basis to Hartwell Construction in November 2025, with a contract sum of £3.84 million and a planned practical completion date of 14 August 2026, so that the new block would be ready for the September intake. Practical completion was certified on 23 October 2026, 70 days late. Pupils were accommodated in temporary classrooms for the first half of the autumn term.

3. Causes of delay
The contractor's delay analysis was reviewed by the Council's independent project manager, who agreed the following allocation of critical-path delay.

Table 1. Critical-path delay by cause
Cause | Days of delay | Responsibility under the contract
Unforeseen ground conditions (old foundations found during excavation) | 21 | Council (relevant event)
Late design changes requested by the school (extra fit-out to two classrooms) | 28 | Council (relevant event)
Delayed delivery of structural steel | 14 | Contractor
Exceptionally wet weather beyond the contract allowance | 7 | Neutral (time but no money)
Total | 70 |

The largest single cause of delay was the unforeseen ground conditions. The site investigation commissioned at feasibility stage used only four trial pits, none of which was located in the footprint of the new hall, where the old foundations were found.

The late design changes arose because the school's requirements for the two classrooms changed after the contract was signed, when the school decided to use them as a specialist resource base. The steel delay arose from the supplier's mill schedule, and the contractor did not identify an alternative supplier.

4. Commercial position
The contract provides for liquidated damages of £2,500 for each day of delay for which the contractor is responsible. The contractor is responsible for 14 days, so the Council will deduct £45,000 in liquidated damages from the final account. The contractor is entitled to an extension of time, but not to additional payment, for the 7 days of exceptional weather.

The final account has been agreed at £4.21 million, an overrun of £370,000 (9.6%) on the contract sum, mainly due to the ground works and the design changes.

5. Comparison with other projects
We compared Riverside with the Council's other education capital projects completed since 2022. The six projects let on a two-stage tender basis finished on average three weeks late, while the five let on a single-stage basis, including Riverside, finished on average nine weeks late. Two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay, and the Council should adopt it as the default procurement route for education projects. The two-stage projects were all refurbishments of existing buildings with budgets under £1.5 million; the single-stage projects were all new-build extensions.

6. Lessons and recommendations
6.1 Adopt two-stage tendering as the default for education capital projects over £1 million.
6.2 Require site investigations to cover the full footprint of any new building, with trial pits or boreholes at each proposed foundation zone.
6.3 Freeze client requirements at contract signature, with any later changes approved by the Director of Education and costed for time and money before instruction.
6.4 Require contractors to identify alternative suppliers for long-lead structural items at tender stage.

7. Conclusion
The delay at Riverside was caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions arising from an inadequate site investigation, compounded by steel supply problems and late changes. Adopting two-stage tendering, together with the specific measures above, would reduce the risk of a recurrence on future projects.
</document>
response:
# Review: Riverside Primary School Extension Delay Review

The review has a clear structure, and the delay table is a useful basis for discussion. However, it has two factual errors and one unsupported causal claim. Each of these affects a headline finding, so all three need fixing before the review goes to Members.

## Critical issues

### 1. The largest cause of delay is the design changes, not the ground conditions

Table 1 gives **28 days** for the late design changes and **21 days** for the ground conditions. Despite this, §3, §7 and your covering note all say ground conditions were "the largest single cause."

The error also skews the narrative:
- The conclusion says the delay was "caused principally by unforeseen ground conditions… compounded by… late changes." That reverses the actual order.
- Both of the two largest causes are Council-side relevant events. Together they account for **49 of the 70 days (70%)**. The review never states this. A Member reading only the conclusion could easily come away thinking the contractor and bad luck were mainly to blame.

**Fix:** Correct §3 and §7, and state plainly that most of the delay was attributable to the Council. Recommendation 6.3 (freezing client requirements) should then come before 6.2, since it addresses the largest cause.

### 2. The liquidated damages figure is wrong

14 days × £2,500 = **£35,000**, not £45,000. The wrong figure appears in §4 and in your covering note. Because it feeds into the final account deduction, it is the most consequential error to correct. Please check that £45,000 hasn't already been notified to Hartwell.

### 3. The two-stage tendering comparison does not support the recommendation

Section 5 itself says the two-stage projects were **all refurbishments under £1.5m** and the single-stage projects were **all new-build extensions**. Procurement route is therefore completely confounded with project type and size:
- New-build carries ground risk; refurbishment largely does not.
- Larger projects tend to overrun by more days in absolute terms.

The data cannot separate the effect of the tendering route from these differences. "Two-stage tendering therefore reduces delay" is not a valid conclusion, and neither is the covering note's "evidence-based case."

There are further weaknesses:
- The sample is very small (6 vs 5 projects).
- Delay is compared in absolute weeks rather than as a percentage of programme.
- Recommendation 6.1 sets the threshold at **over £1m**, yet no two-stage project in the sample exceeded £1.5m. There is no evidence at all for the larger projects the recommendation would mainly affect.

**Fix:** Either remove §5 and 6.1, or reframe them as "two-stage tendering may merit consideration; our data cannot test this because route and project type coincide." A pilot on a new-build project would produce real evidence. Separately, two-stage tendering could plausibly help with Riverside's actual problems, because it allows more design and site investigation to be done before the price is fixed. That argument could be made on its own merits, without the flawed statistics.

## Other points

- **Independence.** The covering note emphasises that the review is independent. However, the Council's project manager is normally the client's agent on the contract. The PM may have administered the very design-change instructions being assessed, so they are not independent of the matters under review. The review is also written by the Capital Projects Team, which commissioned the site investigation it criticises. "Reviewed by the Council's project manager" is accurate; "independent" overstates it. If independence matters to Members, consider an external check of the delay analysis.
- **Concurrency.** The four causes sum neatly to 70 days. This implies they were entirely sequential on the critical path. If any overlapped, particularly the steel delay with the ground works, the contractor's 14 days, and therefore the LDs, could be challenged. The review should state how concurrency was treated.
- **Cost breakdown.** The £370,000 overrun (9.6%, which is correct) is attributed "mainly" to ground works and design changes, but no figures are given. Please split the overrun by cause. Also state whether the contractor has claimed loss and expense for the 49 days of relevant events, since that is typically recoverable and may be part of the £370,000.
- **Wider cost to the Council.** Temporary classroom costs and the disruption to pupils for half a term are not quantified. They are part of the real cost of the delay, and Members will likely ask about them.
- **Root cause of the design changes.** The school changed its plans to use the classrooms as a specialist resource base after contract signature. Freezing requirements (6.3) treats the symptom. Also consider whether the brief-development process consulted the school adequately on likely future needs.

## Verified as correct

- 14 August to 23 October 2026 is 70 days, i.e. ten weeks.
- The Table 1 total is 70 days.
- The final account overrun is £370,000, which is 9.6% of £3.84m.
- The weather treatment (time but no money) is correctly described.

## Summary of required changes

| Section | Change |
|---|---|
| §3, §7 | Design changes (28 days) are the largest cause; state that 49 of 70 days are Council-responsible |
| §4 | LDs = £35,000 |
| §5, 6.1 | Remove the causal claim; acknowledge the confounding; reframe or drop the recommendation |
| §3 | Explain how concurrency was assessed |
| §4 | Break down the overrun by cause; address any loss-and-expense claim |
| Covering note | Drop "independent" or justify it |
